blocks.text: The chapter begins with Sennacherib at Lachish and his envoy confronting Jerusalem. Assyrian royal materials independently portray this campaign: a palace relief cycle shows the assault and capture of Lachish, captives and booty, and Sennacherib enthroned before the city; royal annals claim the capture of Judahite fortified cities, deportations, Hezekiah's confinement in Jerusalem, territorial redistribution, and tribute. These materials help anchor the crisis described here, while their focus on royal victory and their differences from Isaiah's presentation mean they should not be read as neutral, complete transcripts of the campaign.

Isaiah 36 begins a practical reading section often identified as chapters 36–39. The broader divisions of Isaiah can help readers navigate the book, but they are a reading map rather than proof of a single uncontested large-scale structure or a particular number of authors.

sections.title: Where this chapter sits in Isaiah

blocks.text: The confrontation in this chapter turns repeatedly on what Judah and its king will trust: Egyptian military support, Assyrian power, or YHWH. In the Assyrian-era material around this narrative, Isaiah challenges reliance on foreign coalitions and military resources, presenting trust in YHWH as a political as well as religious question.

Isaiah 37 continues the crisis introduced here. A six-sided baked-clay prism inscribed with Sennacherib's royal annals describes his campaign against Judahite fortified cities and his treatment of Hezekiah. It independently situates the figures and conflict of Isaiah 36–37, but its royal perspective should not be treated as a neutral transcript of the biblical narrative.
